newsitem.title: CONGO: France, U.N., U.S. push for peace in Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: France, U.N., U.S. push for peace in Brazzaville.

text.p: The United States, France and the United Nations on Saturday threw their weight behind efforts to end a bloody showdown between Congo's President Pascal Lissouba and former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.

Despite occasional explosions and shooting in the centre of the former French colony's capital, a truce showed signs of taking hold and France prepared to start withdrawing its soldiers after evacuating almost 5,000 foreign nationals.
But a spokesman for Brazzaville mayor and mediator Bernard Kolelas said that the departure of the French troops, due to end their mission on Sunday, would be disastrous for peace hopes.

"If they leave, there will be a terrible battle for the airport, the ceasefire would be ruined and there would be nothing to preserve the gains from negotiations," said the spokesman, Hellot Mampouya. "We really need our French friends to stay, at least to dissuade a return to fighting. They can't abandon us."

Mampouya said French ambassador Raymond Cesaire hosted all-party talks at his residence to try to bring the two main players together for a peace summit in neighbouring fellow oil-producer Gabon with its veteran president, Omar Bongo.
Diplomats said U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun had arrived in Brazzaville and was expected to meet both sides.
The conflict erupted on June 5 after the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a July 27 election.

U.S. Ambassador Aubrey Hooks, who took part in Saturday's talks, told Reuters Television a lull in ethnic and political fighting since Friday was encouraging. "The two sides are talking about concrete steps and that's encouraging," he said.

Kolelas was runner-up to Lissouba in a 1992 presidential election. His supporters were in the thick of fighting that killed at least 2,000 people in 1993 after disputed parliamentary elections. This time they have stayed clear.
He and Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso, both of whom told their forces on Wednesday to cease fire, have said that they want the presidential election to go ahead.
Kolelas and his mediation committee earlier agreed on a peace blueprint envisaging measures such as joint patrols to return the battered city to normal.
Brazzaville enjoyed a relatively calm night after about an hour of sustained shooting around Brazzaville international airport after nightfall. There were reports of shooting in town.
"If you compare what has been happening yesterday and in the night with the last few days then you will definitely say the ceasefire is being respected," Kolelas spokesman Mampouya said.
Diplomats said that the U.S. and French ambassadors began contacts with the various sides two days ago.

Bodies still littered Brazzaville's streets on Friday. Aid workers and military officials had not been able to reach all areas to compile a reliable death toll, which some sources say could run into hundreds and maybe even several thousand.
France said in Paris that it would start pulling its troops out of Brazzaville on Sunday. The government did not say how long the withdrawal would take.
Sassou Nguesso, named president in 1979, bowed to pressure for multi-party politics in 1990 but was among candidates knocked out in the first round of the 1992 poll.
He returned to Congo in January after over a year in France and launched into an undeclared campaign for the presidency.
